Well, for starters, if insurance companies would consider treating chronic mental health cases rather than just focusing on acute cases, it would be helpful.

Only Covering 3 visits to a counselor or a psychiatrist is barely enough time to get a diagnosis, much less a treatment plan.

Furthermore, having better access to solid treatment programs would be helpful. Bust a knee? It's easy to get 6 weeks of PT, but if you melt down, you get 72 hrs in a padded room and a piece of paper showing you where a group may or may not be meeting.

Also, what about recovery assistance? You can insure an arm, or get extended medical leave, but if you go through a divorce that aggrivates an already chronic depression, tough shit, get up and go to work or get fired.

So my association has sent out notice that we're not allowed to put up plywood on the exterior of our condo windows and need to use metal shutters. The problem is that I'm worried I might not have a complete set and might be short a few.

The exterior of the building belongs to them so obviously they don't want people drilling holes into the exterior walls, but if I don't put anything up and there is a hurricane, I risk having the window smashed by a flying projectile along with damaging my property a LOT more than just a few holes in concrete that can be patched up anyway.

It doesn't seem to me that it should be legal to force me to sacrifice my property (interior walls, mold, furniture, wiring, everything) in exchange for comparatively little damage to theirs (holes in stucco that I would be happy to personally patch). It's definitely a dick thing to ask, but can this be fought?
[Florida] Is it legal for my association to ban putting up plywood for a hurricane?
IANAL but I think it would be wise to look at what exactly the written agreement says about this.

A quick review of the Fla HOA statutes seems to show that the only exterior items untouchable by the HOA are the American flag and water conservation landscaping. Sounds like they can restrict pretty much everything else as the board decides.

Since you live in a condo you may look into whether the exterior storm prevention should be a common expense paid for by the HOA. See 718.115(1)(e) The expense of installation, replacement, operation, repair, and maintenance of hurricane shutters, impact glass, code-compliant windows or doors, ... constitutes a common expense and shall be collected as provided in this section if the association is responsible for the maintenance, repair, and replacement of the hurricane shutters, impact glass, code-compliant windows or doors, or other types of code-compliant hurricane protection pursuant to the declaration of condominium. If many are having a hard time finding a complete set of shutters maybe it should be a common item and amended into the covenants or board directives.

As a last ditch effort, if a hurricane is coming, you always have the fallback doctrine of "mitigation of damages" which allows you to take whatever measures necessary to preserve property, notwithstanding those pesky HOA technicalities. I wouldn't rely on this and a fine would surely be forthcoming, but at least you'd have a shot of fighting them from your dry living room which is certainly better than being in compliance with a wet one.

Another thought occurs to me: what declarations has the HOA made to their insurer? Do they declare that all buildings have adequate hurricane protection? If they did, but they don't, may be some leverage for you to obtain those shutters courtesy of the HOA. See if you can get a copy of the policy and use your diplomatic skills. Lying to their insurance company is a nasty bit of misrepresentation no board member would like advertised to their insurer.

This looks like an uphill fight to change the rules, or you could just buy more shutters. Whichever way you decide, good luck!
